10072-english-housewifry-exemplified-in-:
Elizabeth Moxon's English Housewifry gives directions in most parts of cookery in above four hundred and fifty receipts. It teaches soups, cakes, made-dishes, creams, pastes, jellies, pickles, and made-wines, with cuts showing the orderly placing of dishes and courses.

Bills of fare for every month in the year and an alphabetical index complete the book. Moxon calls it necessary for mistresses of families and women servants, confined to things useful, substantial, and splendid. Cooks and historians get eighteenth-century English housekeeping in full, practical detail. Her receipts cover the whole household year.
10097-the-healing-of-nations-and-the-hid:
Edward Carpenter's 1915 book, taking its epigraph from the Tree of Life whose leaves are for the healing of the nations, asks why nations go to war. Chapters examine war-madness, the roots of the Great War, and the case against Germany set beside the case for Germany.

Later chapters weigh patriotism and internationalism, the psychology of war and recruiting, conscription, commercial prosperity as the prosperity of a class, colonies and seaports, and the over-population scare. Carpenter writes as a socialist and pacifist. Readers get a wartime argument for peace, searching and unconventional.
19936-willie-the-waif:
Willie the Waif is a street-child tale in the Hesba Stretton tradition. Its waifs live in rooms they never think to clean. They had never seen their rooms any other way. Dirt had become invisible to them through habit. The pathos of that blindness is the tale's engine. A waif's story promised rescue, reform, or a pious death. Victorian readers wept over such books by the thousand.

Street Arab fiction campaigned for real children's charities. Waifs sold papers, slept in alleys, and died young in fact. Fiction turned those facts into Sunday reading. Willie's story follows the era's tender formula closely. Sentiment here had a social purpose: loosening purse strings. The book is a window into Victorian child-saving feeling.
22890-the-worlds-of-if:
Near disaster haunts The Worlds of If, a story built on a narrow escape. Its narrator reads the evening papers with relief. The liner Baikal, skirting a storm along the eastbound route, had collided mid-air with a British freighter. Only a fifth of her five hundred passengers survived the crash.

He had almost become the late Mr. Wells in a grimmer sense, he jokes, and that joke frames the tale's game with alternate outcomes. What nearly happened matters as much as what did. Stories of this type taught early science fiction readers to think in branching chances. The sea of the air, great liners, and luck fill out a brisk, thoughtful piece.
33241-letters-of-a-lunatic-a-brief-expos:
G. J. Adler's letters tell, in his own words, a strange break in his university life during 1853 and 1854. A professor of German literature in New York, Adler writes of his absence from his proper place of study and of the events that led him away from it. The letters mix personal account with learned allusion, as he tries to set down what happened and why it bore so hard on him.

Printed for the author in 1854, the book is a rare first-person record of a scholar's crisis in the mid-nineteenth century. It reads less as a formal memoir than as a plea to be heard fairly, with dates, names, and scenes set out in plain order. Readers gain a vivid glimpse of academic life, mental strain, and one man's effort to explain himself to the public.
34278-the-secrets-of-potsdam-a-startling:
A courtier turns informer in The Secrets of Potsdam, a startling exposure of the inner life of the courts of the Kaiser and Crown Prince, printed in London in 1917. The London Mail made the book, with two impressions in March of that year. Count Ernst von Heltzendorff, late personal adjutant to the German Crown Prince, reveals the matter. William Le Queux chronicles it.

A letter from the count fronts the book, dated February 10, 1917. He has just finished reading the proofs, he writes, and corrected the two or three small errors. The gross scandals and wily intrigues he related were, many of them, known to Le Queux himself, he notes. The revelations made are but a tithe of the disclosures he could make, he warns. The British public is promised more, if it desires.
35418-lewis-carroll-in-wonderland-and-at:
Belle Moses wrote the life tale of Lewis Carroll at work and at home. The book came out in New York in 1910. Moses had wrote a life of Louisa May Alcott as well. A front plate shows Carroll in a calm, grave pose. She gave the book to two friends named by first marks only.

Her front words say Carroll found a new land on a boat trip. He rowed up and down the river and told a tale as oars dipped. That land took its place in the mind's map for good. No one was quite like him, she tells his friends. The book traces the man behind Alice with warm care.
41012-the-wonderful-story-of-washington-:
The Wonderful Story of Washington and the Meaning of His Life for the Youth and Patriotism of America was written by C. Stevens and copyrighted in nineteen seventeen by Cupples and Leon of New York. Stevens also wrote the Wonderful Story of Lincoln, and the volume joins an Inspiration Series of Patriotic Americans. It opens under a long Webster passage urging American youth to hold up Washington's bright model and study his virtues.

The chapters begin with the meaning of America and Washington's early ground. They follow the boy with a will and a way into border warfare, the struggle for Fort Duquesne, and the slow separation that began between the colonies and England.
41896-dave-fearless-and-the-cave-of-myst:
Dave Fearless and the Cave of Mystery, or Adrift on the Pacific, is a boys sea tale by Rockwood. He had writ past books of the same lad, on a sunk hoard and a float isle. Prints fill this form, put out at New York in the last year of the great war.

Its rights were set in law that same year. A print at its front shows a high cliff and a call to a chief. Its parts run like a yarn log: a fine luck, foul play, a strange named man, and a pair of plot men. A doctors chance harm, a pilots plot, a queer jar, and a foe out wit fill the mid run. A bold plan, a wood isle, and a race for life lead to the sea cast.
52654-the-autobiography-of-goethe-truth-:
The Autobiography of Goethe, in English as Truth and Poetry from My Own Life, is Goethe's account of his own early life. John Oxenford translated it from the German. The revised edition here, from George Bell and Sons in 1897, holds Books One through Twenty in one volume.

An opening note tells the care behind the text. The first ten books had come out in America, but the publisher found that version not faithful enough to the German. Oxenford made a fresh translation, though he kept good renderings from the older one where he found them. The note also weighs the title: Truth and Poetry is the nearest English for Wahrheit und Dichtung. Goethe's own preface follows. For the reader, the book gives the poet's growth in his own words, shaped late in life out of fact and art together.
57667-the-changing-world-and-lectures-to:
Annie Besant lectures in The Changing World and Lectures to Theosophical Students: fifteen lectures delivered in London during May, June, and July 1909. The Theosophical Book Concern of Chicago and the Theosophical Publishing Society of London issued them in 1910. Besant was president of the Theosophical Society.

Part one, lectures to the public, opens with the deadlock in religion, science, and art. It turns to the new doors opening, brotherhood applied to social conditions, the coming race, and the coming Christ. Part two speaks to students: the sixth sub-race, the sacramental life, and the nature of the Christ.
62745-dissertation-on-the-gipseys-repres:
H M G Grellmann's German study of the Gypsy people reached English readers in a new form in 1807. William Ballintine printed it at London. This printing trims the heavy notes of the first translation by M Raper.

The contents map a whole way of life. Early chapters treat names, food, and drink. Then come dress, family economy, and trades. Marriages and schooling follow. Sickness, death, and burial get their own chapters. Grellmann also asks where this people came from. His closing enquiry traces their origin and first steps into Europe. The work shaped how Europe saw the Romani for a century. Modern readers use it with care, as a record of its age as much as of its subject.
64345-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art began its fifth series with number one on Saturday, January 5, 1884. William and Robert Chambers had founded the journal in 1832. This issue, priced at three halfpence, opens with a story called By Mead and Stream, by Charles Gibbon, author of Robin Gray.

Gibbon's first chapter, headed Much Virtue in If, muses on lives looking back from a hilltop. Old friends meet and sigh over the word if: the road not taken, the advice not given in time. The scene sets a reflective tone for a weekly that mixed fiction with science and art for family reading. The Chambers firm built its name on cheap, improving print for the new reading public.
64475-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, for Saturday 12 January 1884, is number two of the first volume of its fifth series. The paper was set up by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. It was run by R. Chambers the second, and sold for a penny halfpenny. The lead piece asks a plain question: What is a peer?

Many folk seem to think, the piece says, that each man called Lord So-and-so is a peer. That notion is wholly wrong, it holds. The peerage of this realm, unlike that of other lands, is a matter of real weight, in a social and in a state sense. So an answer to the question may not prove dull, the piece goes on. The word peer itself, in its root sense, hints at no high place at all, it notes with surprise.
64571-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number three of its fifth series, is a weekly issue dated Saturday, January 19, 1884. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in 1832. The price was three halfpence. The lead article is an essay on the training of girls, wives, and mothers among the middle classes.

The writer grants that higher culture for women draws much sympathy in theory. In practice, the essay warns, schools give drawing room polish at the cost of home skill. Young housewives gain too much of the stage and too little of the kitchen. The author argues that training should fit women for the battle of life. For middle class women, those years of battle come after marriage, not before. Education, on this view, must not end at the altar.
64962-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal gave London readers a cheap weekly of tale and fact. Issue five of the fifth series is dated February 2, 1884. It sold for one and a half pence. William and Robert Chambers set the paper up in 1832. A younger Chambers ran it at this date.

Hampstead Heath leads with tales of boy days on its wild edge. Ass rides and wild rides through fern scared nurses then, it says. The old town on the hill still keeps its own ways, it holds. A fifth of November march winds its steep streets each year. More tale and science bits fill the rest.
64993-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 7 of volume I, fifth series, is a weekly number dated Saturday, February 16, 1884. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in 1832. R Chambers (Secundus) conducted this series. The price was three-halfpence. The number leads with an article on life assurance: How Life-Offices Pay Their Death-Claims.

The article answers an old objection to life assurance, the delay in paying claims. Offices now vie, it says, in prompt settlement. Policies already provide some four hundred and thirty-five millions sterling for future widows and orphans. That figure excludes industrial business. The writer marvels at the alleviation of misery the sum represents. Cottages and stately halls alike draw on the beneficent treasury. Popular misunderstandings still abound, the article notes. One man proposed to draw half his assurance at once. Another asked to let his premiums run as a debt against the policy.
64994-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 4 of its fifth series, is dated Saturday, January 26, 1884. William and Robert Chambers founded the weekly in 1832. R Chambers, the second of that name, now conducts it. The number leads with an editorial, Another Word to Literary Beginners. The editors address the great class knocking weekly at literature's doors.

They back the warning with their own submission figures. From August 1882 to August 1883 they received 3,225 manuscripts. Of these, 2,065 were prose and 1,160 verse. They accepted 300 prose pieces, about fourteen per cent. Only 30 poems passed, under three per cent. Ten of every hundred manuscripts were kept, and ninety returned. The offerings came from across the English-speaking world. They ranged from a few stanzas to a three-volume novel. The editorial urges encouragement within limits. Most aspirants, it warns, harvest only disappointment and heart-sickness.
65015-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal for Saturday, February 23, 1884, is number eight of the first volume of its fifth series. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in 1832, and it sold for three halfpence. Popular literature, science, and art fill its stated scope.

The number leads with Our Health, a lecture series by Andrew Wilson, a health lecturer. Health, Wilson says, is the smooth working of all the body's organs in concert. A broken bone breaks that harmony just as a fever does, and an aching tooth counts as much as a brain disorder. Life hangs on surroundings, he notes, and those can turn from support to source of disease. Pure air and clean water, both needs of life, can carry sickness when fouled. The lecture sets out to teach readers their own machinery.
65133-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 10 of the fifth series, is a weekly magazine issue. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in the year 1832. Chambers the second conducted this series from Edinburgh in Scotland. This number is dated Saturday, March 8, 1884, at three halfpence. Nettle Cloth, its lead article, opens on a botanist's remark.

A famous botanist was asked about gathering all plants used in medicine. Such a hoard would take a large building to hold, he replied. Fibre yielding plants would still form a long list for study. Very few serve for clothing among civilised and savage races alike. Cotton and flax hold prime importance, the article argues, with hemp rising.
65209-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, fifth series, number eleven, is the issue for Saturday, March 15, 1884. The journal was founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832, and now conducted by a later Chambers. The price was three halfpence. The lead tale is Happy Ever After.

By firelight, children have heard a traveller tale of the desert mirage. Tufted palms, green herbage, water, shade, and rest promise at a distance, then flee from pursuit. A little voice from the hearthrug pipes up in protest. Golden hair glistens round a dissatisfied face as the child demands a fairy tale instead. The teller must reach the set ending, that they were happy ever after. Then the child asks if they were perfectly happy, and if there was never a wet day. Readers get a family weekly tale that plays with its own ending.
65239-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number twelve of its fifth series, is a weekly issue dated Saturday, March 22, 1884. The journal had been founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. The price was three halfpence. The lead article reports on the gold fields of the Transvaal, written by a man on the spot.

The writer says the fields have drawn fresh notice at home and in South Africa. Gold lies scattered over a wide country, reaching toward the Zambesi river. The busiest belt runs from the Kaap River north past Pilgrim's Rest. Named farms there have yielded the largest amounts so far. Most gold found is loose in the soil and won by washing with water. Two companies were starting to crush quartz rock with machines when he wrote.
65279-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal dated this weekly number Saturday, March 29, 1884, in its fifth series, first volume. The paper had been founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. Its lead article turns to the International Forestry Exhibition planned for Edinburgh in 1884.

The writer begins with the age of great exhibitions, which newspapers call a wholesome mania. He asks what calls such shows into being and what good their backers expect from them. Towns, host countries and all the nations taking part stand to gain, he argues, if the show is well aimed and honestly run.
65389-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal number 15 of its fifth series came out April 12, 1884. William and Robert Chambers founded the weekly back in 1832. The price was a penny and a half for this issue. Its lead piece treats nature in the country round London.

The piece draws on Richard Jefferies and his book Nature Near London. It says fine villages and lanes lie just twelve miles out. Bird and insect life fill copses, brooks, and green lanes there. A great trout in a beech shaded pool held the author gaze for years. This number is the fifteenth of the journal's fifth series.
65543-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 16 of the fifth series, volume 1, was dated Saturday, April 19, 1884. The weekly, founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832, was now conducted by a second Robert Chambers. The lead essay, Sudden Fortunes, opens with tales of wealth gained in a flash.

The essay notes how gold and diamond fields and big lottery prizes grip readers. When French state lotteries ended in 1837, Alphonse Karr protested that five sous bought the poorest man a chance to be a millionaire, and killing the chance killed a ray of hope. Set gains from trade or kin apart, the essay says: true sudden fortune drops, unlooked for, into a man's hands like a bird or a pearl.
65567-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal for Saturday, April 26, 1884, is number 17 of the fifth series, priced at a penny halfpenny. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in 1832. The lead article takes up post-office life assurance and annuities. The scheme had run since 1865 to help the poorer classes save.

Its results, the journal admits, are trifling. In nearly twenty years only six thousand five hundred and twenty-four life policies were issued. Annuity contracts reached twelve thousand four hundred and thirty-five. Live policies had sunk to four thousand six hundred and fifteen. A committee under the Postmaster-General Fawcett reported in 1882, and an act passed the same session. The new system was to start on the first of May.
65647-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 20 of its fifth series, came out on Saturday, May 17, 1884, at a penny-halfpenny. The weekly had been founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832 and was now conducted by Chambers the second. Its lead paper, Some Curiosities of the Peerage, is the first of two parts.

That earlier paper dealt with the outside of the institution: the peerage, the House of Lords, and real against courtesy titles. This paper turns inward, to the oddities known only to the few: family vicissitudes, personal anecdotes, and the strange workings of the system. The writer argues that no one can fully grasp the history of the country, general or constitutional, without knowing the peerage and how it works. Instruction, he promises, will come wrapped in amusement.
65679-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, fifth series, number 21 of volume one, dated Saturday, May 24, 1884, price one penny halfpenny, was conducted by R Chambers the second. The journal was established by William and Robert Chambers in 1832.

The number opens with From Jaffa to Jerusalem. Coasting the arid Syrian shore from Port Said, the traveller first knows Jaffa by a powerful perfume of orange-flowers borne across the sea. The whitened, flat-roofed town rises abruptly from its reef-guarded harbour, by the fabled rocks of Andromeda's captivity. Boats piled with oranges, lemons, and melons crowd round the steamer at the quay.
65723-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 22 of the fifth series, is a weekly magazine issue. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in the year 1832. Chambers the second conducted this series from Edinburgh in Scotland. This number is dated Saturday, May 31, 1884, at three halfpence. Its lead article, Our Detective Police, opens the number's argument.

Many murders near London have gone unsolved in the last few months. Few murderers have been brought to justice in that span, it says. Thefts and burglaries beyond count go unpunished, since culprits vanish unseen. London's boast as the safest city in the world rings hollow here. A new departure in detective police is required, the writer urges.
65785-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
A weekly journal of popular reading, founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832, reached number twenty three of its fifth series on June 7, 1884. The price was three halfpence. The lead piece is a character sketch of the newsmonger. He is nothing, the writer says, if not all knowing.

When a bankruptcy bursts on the world, the newsmonger is never surprised. He knew it weeks before, down to the sum and the chief creditor. When a wife runs off, he had warned both parties. When an engagement breaks, he advised the break himself. He deals in bad news by choice, for it has the spice that good news lacks. The sketch is dry, fond, and cutting, a fair sample of the journal's fare for the fireside.
65795-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, Fifth Series, Number 24 for June 14, 1884, was sold at three halfpence. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in 1832. R Chambers the second ran this issue. The lead piece treats St Marguerite and St Honorat, isles in the Mediterranean.

The piece notes a sad link to the Duke of Albany. His last public act was to sign a plea against the sale of St Marguerite. The isles lie in the Golfe de Frejus off Cannes. Tales of the man with the iron mask hang over St Marguerite. Old tales say a young knight from Gaul first settled the isles in early Christian days. His sister Marguerite followed him there.
65828-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
A weekly number of a long-running magazine fills this item: Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, fifth series, number twenty-six, dated Saturday, June 28, 1884. The journal was founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. This number opens with the third paper of a health series by Andrew Wilson: some food-dangers, and how to avoid them.

Wilson ranks impure food beside impure air and water as a cause of illness. Adulteration fills his charge sheet. Alum and copper salts go into bread, water and treacle into milk, and black-lead and clay into faced tea. Green peas preserved in tins carry copper too. Such fraud, he argues, cries out for laws against it.
65862-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art is a weekly magazine founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. The hosted issue opens the fifth series, dated Saturday, July 5, 1884, and priced at a penny halfpenny. It was conducted by Robert Chambers the second. The lead article is the first of a series on home nursing, written by a lady.

That article argues that illness visits every household, so care of the sick matters to all. It notes how trained nursing has lately improved, pushing out the old careless nurse of story. Yet most people still know little of bedside care, and the series aims to teach them. It stresses plain guidance so a reader can act in an emergency with some skill. The journal mixed such practical pieces with literature, science, and art for a broad public.
65881-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal, number twenty eight of the fifth series, is a weekly from July twelfth eighteen eighty four. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in eighteen thirty two. Chambers the second conducted this series of the popular weekly. The price was three halfpence for the number that week in Britain.

The lead piece, On Moor and Loch, opens at a small Scottish station. A June morning follows a fortnight drought and two days of kind rain. Grey mist, or haar, rolls in from the German Ocean on east wind. No angler loves mist, the writer notes, for trout gain by its cover. Pentland hills loom as a darker bank in a grey waste of cloud.
65883-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal for Saturday, July 19, 1884, is the twenty-ninth number of the journal's fifth series. William and Robert Chambers founded the weekly in 1832, and it sold for three halfpence. Its lead essay is Some Cheering Aspects of Mortality. The essay takes up a grim subject with dry wit.

The writer says we always mourn what the world loses when great men die. We seldom credit what the world gains by their going. Leading men who live too long can block the way of the next generation. Even our own shoes may be better filled after us. The essay also notes that the great are often scorned in life. Distance alone lends them their glow, and honor comes only after death.
65951-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art is a week sheet set up by William and Robert Chambers in eighteen thirty two. The host print is count thirty of the fifth line of the sheet. It bears the date of a high day of eighteen eighty four. Its price is set at the head of the page. A man of the same name runs the sheet.

The lead piece of the week treats a Scots sea watch post. The sea, it says, has been watched for ages in more ways than men can count. Bards have sung of it, fish men have fished it, sea men have sailed it for years past count. Yet it is still a tract of doubt and awe. The lore of the sea is yet in its young years.
66007-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal for a day in the summer of eighteen eighty four is one issue of a cheap weekly of tales, science, and art. This is its fifth run, set up by its two first hands in the age of Victoria as a girl. A grand son of one of them now runs the sheet.

Its lead piece is a plain talk on water. Water bears a most big part in the frame of man and the keep of health, it says. It joins with the stuff of the body and forms a need part of its build. In a man of a set weight, it gives the pounds of him that are water. It goes deep in the make of our food as well. Yet few folk, it holds, have sound lore of its first springs.
66097-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, fifth series number 33, dated Saturday, August 16, 1884, price three halfpence, leads with Cave-Chapels. In the lives of the early Celtic saints, the article says, it is often recorded that they ended their days in seclusion.

They left their monasteries for a lonely island or mountain solitude, to pass life's evening in undisturbed devotion. Joceline's Life of St Kentigern records his custom of retiring to a cave during Lent, to hide himself in God. Such retreats were called Deserta, a word surviving in the place-names Dysart and Disert across Scotland and Ireland. Readers get the great cheap weekly tracing hermits' caves into modern maps.
66127-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, in its fifth series under R Chambers, leads its number for Saturday, August 23, 1884, with an article on grouse. The journal, founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832, sold this weekly number at three-halfpence. The grouse piece opens with market figures: as many as five hundred thousand birds reach the markets each year.

On some August days, the article reports, sixteen thousand grouse arrive at the London wholesale dealers in a single day. It then turns to the bird's powers of recovery after disease, the usual seven to nine eggs in a nest, and the crows, stoats and weasels that prey on the brood.
66141-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, fifth series, number 35, dated Saturday, August 30, 1884, price three halfpence. The journal was founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832 and by then was run by a second Robert Chambers.

The lead article, A River Holiday, covers the annual sailing-barge match from Erith to the Nore and back. It calls the race the great day of the riverside people below bridge, as Henley is to the upper Thames. The writer boards the little Cygnet at Blackwall pier among excursion crowds, bound for a dozen hours on the river. Readers get a bright slice of Victorian holiday life on the working Thames.
66175-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
The hosted text is one weekly number of Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, in its fifth series. The issue is number 36 of volume one, dated Saturday, September 6, 1884, and priced at three halfpence. The journal was founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832.

The number is conducted by a later member of the Chambers family. Its lead article, headed Grand Day, takes up the call to the bar. It explains that the phrase puzzles most outsiders. There is in fact no calling, beyond the reading of the names of the men put forward. There is no bar of any kind used in the rite. The article goes on to the dinners law students must eat and the fun of the circuit mess.
66232-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
One weekly number of Chambers's Journal, dated Saturday, September 20, 1884, forms the hosted text. The journal was founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832, and this fifth-series number sold for three halfpence. R Chambers the second conducted the paper at this date.

The number opens with a life of Dr Jenner, set off by the moving of his statue from Trafalgar Square to Kensington Gardens. The piece traces Jenner's path from a Berkeley apprenticeship to the milkmaid's remark that cowpox guards against smallpox. It quotes John Hunter's advice to the young doctor, not to think but to try, and to be patient and exact. Readers get a sample of the improving weekly fare Victorian families read at home.
66236-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Number 37 of Chambers's Journal, fifth series, came out on Saturday, September 13, 1884. Chambers the second still ran the paper his house founded in 1832. Joint-stock companies and limited liability lead the number, a dry head for a live fraud age.

Newspaper readers know the long prospectuses in the ads, the piece begins. They sing in rosy terms why a new company deserves men's money. Mines of tin or silver, patented goods, land loans, banks, tramways: the forms run on without end. Prairie cattle in the Far West stand in the list of lures. The piece asks what the limited form guards, and what it lets loose. Plain talk for small savers in the great age of the bubble company.
66267-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal for Saturday, September twenty-seventh, eighteen eighty-four, is number thirty-nine of volume one, fifth series. R Chambers, the second of that name, ran the journal, founded in eighteen thirty-two. The lead piece is the third article on home-nursing, by a lady.

Earlier papers chose the sick-room; this one treats its running. Heavy woollen hangings, the writer warns, hold dust and bad smells. Lace or light washing curtains serve better. Simple wooden chairs with cane seats are best, and a chair-bed will do for a sofa. Carpets may stay, she holds, since they spare noise and keep the room natural. Cupboards must never hold food or soiled things.

72929-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, fifth series number 135, for Saturday, July 31, 1886, sold at three-halfpence under Robert Chambers the second. The journal had been established by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. The lead essay, Hygeia in the Dog-Days, muses on the goddess of health while the thermometer stands above eighty in the shade. The writer confesses to regaling himself not wisely but too well on hot foods, because he liked them.

Hygeia, pictured on a marble column like an Alma-Tadema painting, waves her hand over the smoking viands and preaches abstention: milk and water, grapes and strawberries, and no alcohol in the heat. The essay catalogues the broiling-day dinner it renounces: hot roast duck, hot vegetables, stout, plum pudding, and whisky toddy. The tone is the journal's family miscellany manner, moralising with a pipe in hand.
72935-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art is a weekly magazine number dated Saturday, August 7, 1886. The journal was founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832, its masthead says. This number, priced at three halfpence, is number 136 of the third volume of its fifth series. It opens with a nature piece by Richard Jefferies called Winds of Heaven.

Jefferies watches a still day break into wind. The window rattles, the gate swings, and a leaf rises for the kitten to chase. Folded shutters shake and a kitchen latch rattles as if a hand moved through the house. Then calm returns: the kitten curled in sunshine, a sparrow at the rose tree, a bee on a dandelion. The whole piece turns on such small signs, in Jefferies' close watching manner.
73319-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal gave town readers a cheap weekly of tale, science, and art. This issue, number 138, is dated August 21, 1886. It sold for one and a half pence in the fifth series. William and Robert Chambers set the paper up in 1832. A younger Chambers ran it at this date.

73395-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal, number 139 of the fifth series, is the issue for Saturday, 28 August 1886. The journal of popular literature, science, and art was established by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. Chambers the second conducts the volume, and the price is three halfpence. The number opens with an essay called Our Ways and Theirs.

To do at Rome as the Romans do is sage advice, the essay begins for its readers. It is not always nor often followed by those of us who wander afield, it adds in its argument. We place ourselves among people whose ways and habits differ from our own in travel. Principles stricter than our own we call prejudices in the essay rebuke of the English traveller. The weekly number mixes that sermon on manners with the tales and science of the week, in the Chambers manner of instruction with entertainment.
73792-eric-a-waif:
Eric, a Waif is a story of the last century by Emma Leslie, published by the Religious Tract Society in London. The tale is set in Summerleigh, a village on the edge of Epping Forest that guards itself jealously against strangers. Young Eric Hunter's mother, a poor widow who sold herbs and salves from her cottage, was rumoured a witch by the neighbours.

The opening chapter finds the village gossiping over her death at the Magpie inn. The landlord asks after the boy, left alone at ten years old, while the company grumbles that the pair should have stayed in their own parish. Chapter titles promise a voyage and a new home for the orphan.
73956-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:

Beech and fir rings mark the park edge in that still scene. Pigeon coo and lark song fill its dusk close in rich sound.
73978-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:

74146-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:

74223-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 143 of volume three, fifth series, is dated Saturday, September 25, 1886. Founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832, it is here conducted by a second Robert Chambers. The first piece is a year's postal work. Government blue-books are dull enough to the ordinary reader, it opens, but the yearly report of the Postmaster-General is at once curious and of interest.

The growth of the postal system, the article holds, marks both the trade growth of the nation and the spread of schooling. It then sums up the report for the year ending March 31, 1886. Letters delivered in the United Kingdom alone reach a total of over fourteen hundred million. Cards, packets, papers, and parcels swell the grand total past two thousand million items. About fifty-one thousand officers form the standing staff.
74500-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of popular literature, science and art reaches number 144 of its fifth series here. It appeared on Saturday, October 2, 1886, from the Edinburgh house founded in 1832. An article called 'Truth in the Marvellous' opens the number at the front of the issue.

Antiquarian research has dealt cruel blows at time-honoured traditions, it begins in warning. Troy itself never existed, we are taught, and Arthur's Round Table was a myth, the essay lists. Godiva never rode naked through Coventry, and Joan of Arc was never burned but married happily, such debunking leaves readers hardly knowing what to believe.
75204-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers’s Journal number 146, dated Saturday, October 16, 1886, belongs to the third volume of its fifth series. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in 1832. It sold at three halfpence a number in that year. The lead article is Cave Hunting in Yorkshire, a piece of local exploration.

The finest county in all England is the great shire of York, it begins. Rugged coast, rolling plains, and noble churches are praised in that opening. Wild moorlands, lofty fells, and fertile valleys with monastic ruins follow. Every Yorkshireman is proud of his county, the writer declares. Squire, merchant prince, artisan, and dalesman share that pride in his list. The journal mixed such essays with tales and facts for family reading.
75211-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal for October 23, 1886 is number 147 of the journal's fifth series, priced at three halfpence. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in 1832. The issue opens with The Maoris' Fight for Life, by a New Zealander. It calls the Maori story an absorbing struggle of life and death.

A gallant and interesting people, the writer says, are making a last stand for existence. He counts barely forty thousand Maoris left in the colony. In 1835, before settlement began in earnest, careful observers reckoned near two hundred thousand. Captain Cook had guessed four hundred thousand. The article traces that fall and asks what it means.
75329-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
This number of Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, fifth series, is No 148, Vol III, dated Saturday, October 30, 1886, price 1½d. The journal was established by William and Robert Chambers in 1832 and is conducted here by R Chambers (Secundus). Its lead article takes up the Matterhorn and its victims. The peak, fourteen thousand seven hundred and eighty feet high, stands alone among the Pennine Alps, and the writer says no other single peak approaches it in grandeur of shape.

The article recalls the peasants' old dread of the haunted mountain and Edward Whymper's long, costly campaign of failed attempts before he reached the summit. Earlier tries by Val Tournanche guides from 1858 onward reached no higher than twelve thousand six hundred and fifty feet.
75449-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Number 149 of a family weekly dates to Saturday, November 6, 1886. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in 1832. R Chambers the second conducts its fifth series. The price is three halfpence.

Notes on the New Hebrides lead the number. The group stretches about seven hundred miles in the western Pacific. Espiritu Santo, the largest island, runs seventy-five miles by forty. The whole land area comes to about five thousand square miles. Estimates of the people run from fifty thousand to two hundred thousand. Some thirty languages sound across the group, all akin in grammar, none understood by the next island. The writer notes Papuan traits with traces of Polynesian mixture. On Vaté the men stand taller and fairer. France's interest gave the islands their news value.
75656-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, fifth series, number 150, dated Saturday, November 13, 1886, price three halfpence. The lead article describes the portable theatre, the traveling playhouse of small Victorian towns.

Meet its wagons on the highway, the writer says, and you know it by the shutters, poles, seat-planks, and painted canvas. Actor-builders dig holes, raise the frame, drape the walls, and spread sawdust, then wash and shave in time to perform that night. The Hamlet of a quarter to eight was hauling timber at seven. Companies worked on nightly shares, each player a small partner. Readers get a backstage look at popular theater at its most makeshift.
75692-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of popular literature, science and art was founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. This number, 151 of the fifth series, appeared on Saturday, November 20, 1886. An article called 'Nothing New' opens the number at the front of the issue.

Antiquaries love to remind us there is nothing new under the sun, it begins. Printing brings the Chinese in as evidence against European pride, the essay argues. Romans used movable types to mark pottery and bread, it goes on. The Assyrians cut a rock-crystal magnifying lens that Brewster praised, found amid the ruins of Nimroud, in a penny paper's wide net.
75818-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal opened its Number 152 with a study of sealskin coats, alive and dead. The issue is dated Saturday, November 27, 1886, and sold for a penny and a half. R Chambers the second ran the fifth series of the journal. The piece draws chiefly on H W Elliott of the Smithsonian.

Elliott watched fur seals for three years on the Pribylov Islands of Alaska. The islands lie in Behring Sea, found by a Russian sailor in 1786. Reckless killing had near wiped out the southern herds, the piece warns. Readers learn how a fine coat starts as a wild beast's life.
75937-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal dated this weekly number Saturday, December 4, 1886, in its fifth series. The lead article goes on guard at Windsor Castle with the soldiers there. Guarding the sovereign's chief residence is an honor, the writer grants at the start of the piece.

Yet soldiers do not rate the duty highly, he says plainly in the article. Windsor guard duty is hard, meaning few nights in bed for the men on sentry-go. At some stations men get as many as twenty such nights in a row; at Windsor, the writer passed every third night on the exposed terraces of the castle.
76348-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Number 154 of the fifth series of Chambers's Journal, dated Saturday, December 11, 1886. The journal, founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832, was now conducted by a second Robert Chambers. Its lead article treats inn-signs, their origin and meanings. In times past, the writer says, signs were not ornaments but necessities. When few could read, a tradesman's name over his door meant nothing, while a painted device marked his house and often his wares.

The article reads the surviving signs as history: they speak of the customs and superstitions of our forefathers, the party strifes they engaged in, and the great men who made English history. The journal mixed such essays with stories and facts for its vast weekly readership, the penny press at its most respectable.
76956-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 155 of the fifth series, is the issue dated Saturday, December 18, 1886. The journal dated its founding by William and Robert Chambers to 1832. The lead piece, Just Before Winter, came from Richard Jefferies. He had written The Gamekeeper at Home. Russet deepens on the forest top like a stain, he writes. Leaves make the year's last crop. Red heath, pale larch, and deep blue sky fill the hill.

Jefferies notes ferns still green in sheltered lanes. Herb Robert and bramble leaves turn scarlet and crimson. Furze shows a second bloom after the frosts pause. He watches buds that might open again if sun returned. The piece is close nature writing at the turn of the year.
77054-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chamberss Journal for December the twenty fifth of eighteen eighty six is one weekly issue. This copy is number one hundred and fifty six of the third volume. The sheet sold for three half pence in the Chambers line. Christmas day bore the date of this late year issue.

The unseen parts of a theatre lead the issue with a back stage tour. Rooms high and low past the screen dwarf what the crowd sees, it says. A great Paris house that burnt had four floors dug deep in earth. Tales, verse, and fact notes fill the rest of the cheap weekly sheet. The journal served home shelves with bright sound fare each week.
britannica-1911-abdallatif:
Abdallatif receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abdallatif, a Bagdad-born doctor and traveller of 1162, left his own memoir, kept by a contemporary. Grammar, Koran, and Arabian poetry formed the youth of Bagdad, and he mastered them before turning to nature and medicine.

Mosul, Damascus, and Egypt drew him for learned company; Maimonides, the Eagle of the Doctors, granted the talk he craved. Saladin's circle at Jerusalem took him in. Teaching at Cairo, Damascus, and Aleppo filled his years, and late travel crossed Armenia and Asia Minor. Death caught him at Bagdad in 1231, bound for Mecca. Of his many works, one Account of Egypt lives in Europe, with its famine tale from a failed Nile flood.
britannica-1911-coif:
A coif is a close cap for the head, from a French word for a cap. In the middle ages men and women wore it out of doors. It tied under the chin like a night-cap. Later men kept it as a night-cap or skull-cap at home. One form of the cap gained a set place in English law.

Serjeants-at-law wore a coif of white lawn or silk as a mark of their rank. Fashion added a small black skull-cap on top of the white. When wigs came in at the end of the 1600s, a round space was left bare on top. The coif showed through that space. In time a patch of black silk edged with white took its place. The entry rejects a guess that the cap first hid the church tonsure. That tale, it says, rests on no proof.
britannica-1911-massif: Massif is a French term adopted in geology and in physical geography, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains in brief. It names a mountainous mass or a group of connected heights in the land. Such a mass may stand isolated on its own in a region. Or it may form part of a larger mountain system as one block. A massif is more or less clearly marked off by the valleys that surround it on its sides.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-wyclif:
John Wyclif was the Oxford theologian called the Morning Star of the Reformation, whose teachings anticipated Protestant reform. Born probably at Hipswell in Yorkshire in 1324, he was educated at Balliol College and resigned its mastership in 1361 for the living of Fillingham, later exchanged for Ludgershall. He took his doctorate in theology probably in 1372, holding the rich living of Lutterworth from 1373.

The entry untangles his early career from another man of the same name, including the disputed wardenship of Canterbury Hall under Archbishop Islip. There the warden was ousted for a monk and lost his appeal to Rome. From his Oxford eminence Wyclif launched the attacks on papal wealth, friars, and transubstantiation that made him famous and condemned. He died at Lutterworth on the last day of 1384, his bones later dug up and burned by order of the Council of Constance.
doe-osti-2572204-microwave-catalysis-for:
Final technical report DE-FE-0031866, from West Virginia University under John Hu, is dated July 17, 2025. Partners were North Carolina State, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, H-Quest Vanguard, C4-MCP, and Southern California Gas. The project built a modular microwave reactor that turns natural gas directly into carbon nanotubes, carbon fibers, and hydrogen. The chemistry splits methane into solid carbon and hydrogen gas, emitting no carbon dioxide.

Catalyst design took up much of the work, since commercial catalysts are not made for microwave reactors. Families tested include nickel catalysts on carbon nanotubes and several perovskite-style oxides carrying nickel or cobalt. A variable-frequency microwave reactor was built and run, and a separation step recovered catalyst from the carbon products for reuse. The modular unit showed a wide turndown ratio, so it can keep working as flare gas flow and makeup vary at a field site.
doe-osti-2575072-code-coverage-status-of:
Argonne report ANL/NSE-23/65, revision 1, by Zhaopeng Zhong, Michael A. Smith, and Changho Lee, audits how much of the DIF3D code the test suite actually runs. DIF3D is the neutronics workhorse of the Argonne Reactor Code system, used for forty years on fast and thermal reactor design. Recent verification covered the geometry options used by the Versatile Test Reactor project, but only for the paths those tests touched.

The team built test problems and measured coverage across the code's subroutines and source folders. Priority went to DIF3D-VARIANT and DIF3D-FD, the paths designers actually use. DIF3D-Nodal was inspected as well. The point is regression safety: a code path no test runs can hide an error for years. The report maps which parts are touched and which are not, so future tests can close the gaps on purpose.
doe-osti-2997601-hydraulic-testing-of-th:
Kenneth Dixon reports pump testing of a cleanup well at the Savannah River Site, in Savannah River report SRNL-STI-2025-00306 dated September 2025. Recovery well RWM001R draws from the Lost Lake Aquifer Zone to capture contaminated groundwater. Testing set the well's baseline performance and the aquifer's hydraulic conductivity, the ease with which water moves through it.

Two step-drawdown tests and two constant-rate tests ran in March 2025, the constant-rate run lasting 13 days from 27 March. At the pump's capacity of about 54 gallons per minute, average specific capacity was 2.2 gallons per minute per foot of drawdown. Well efficiency averaged 56 percent at full rate, rising to about 79 percent at gentler rates. Odd water level wiggles in observation wells cut the long test short, and the aquifer was left to recover. Cleanup designers size pumps and spacing from these figures.
doe-osti-2997621-searching-for-phase-tra:
Yeanwoo Park hunts for phase transitions in artificial kagome spin ice, in Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-29741, issued 30 September 2025. Spin ice is a pattern of tiny magnets whose north-south frustrations mimic the disorder of water ice. The kagome version arranges the magnets on a woven lattice of triangles and hexagons, a geometry known for strange collective states.

Magnetic force microscopy supplies the pictures: a fine needle on a cantilever taps across the surface, and a laser bounced off the lever reads its deflections. That gives both the surface shape and the magnetic pattern island by island. Watching the pattern reorganize with field or temperature is how a phase change would show itself. The report assembles the method and the search, a step toward designer magnetic materials whose states can be set on purpose.
doe-osti-3031149-legacy-metallic-fuel-u-:
Kun Mo of Argonne National Laboratory, Aaron Oaks, Carolyn Tomchik, and colleagues from Argonne and Idaho present this July 2025 report on old fast reactor fuel data. The Metallic Fuels Irradiation and Physics Database holds records for uranium-plutonium-zirconium fuel from the Experimental Breeder Reactor II and the Fast Flux Test Facility. New reactor designers want to trust that legacy data, so its quality must be checked in a formal way.

The database holds three data kinds: fuel pin fabrication specs, running conditions such as power and burnup along each pin, and post-irradiation exam results like gas release and chemistry. The check follows Argonne quality plan, which the Nuclear Regulatory Commission reviewed in 2019 and confirmed in 2020. Peer review by fuel experts is the chosen method for judging each record.
doe-osti-3422384-mixing-zone-dilution-st:
Pacific Northwest report, dated April 2026, studies how discharge water mixes and dilutes near the lab's Sequim Campus. L. T. Premathilake and T. P. Khangaonkar wrote the mixing zone study. State rules set how dilution must be figured for permits.

Worst-case flow was set at the pump maximum of 175 gallons per minute. Daily records for 2023 show discharge came in bursts, not steady flow. Monthly averages drew on six years of data. Dilution at the worst case then decides permit limits. Campus staff get a defensible basis for discharge terms. Six years of flow records anchor the dilution calculations presented in this study.
english-housewifry-exemplified-in-above-:
Elizabeth Moxon offers above four hundred and fifty receipts in English Housewifry, the fruit, she says, of thirty years of practice and experience. Directions cover soups, cakes, made dishes, creams, pastes, jellies, pickles, and made wines. Cuts show the orderly placing of dishes and courses, and bills of fare run for every month of the year.

Receipt 270 makes calf's foot flummery: boil two dressed feet in two quarts of water till half is consumed, then set, chill, and turn out pricked with blanched almonds. An appendix adds sixty more receipts from skilled gentlewomen nearby. Moxon writes for mistresses of families and women servants, on measures of frugality. The book stands among the plainest, most used cookbooks of its century.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ClayCassius_Cla:
Cassius Marcellus Clay of Kentucky was the nineteenth century's most combative abolitionist, a slaveholder's son who turned against slavery and fought duels over emancipation. This essay, by an unidentified author, celebrates him under the name Muhammad Ali was born with.

The essay praises Clay as 'the greatest' across fighting, editorials, and even husbands, in the loose and hearty style of a magazine tribute. Clay edited an abolitionist paper, survived attempts on his life, and lived to be a legend called the Lion of White Hall. The piece survives as popular biography, more affectionate than exact, preserved in the research files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NavyFOIALiftonR:
The Chief of Naval Operations sent this memorandum on February 25, 1981. It refers Harold Weisberg's freedom-of-information request onward to the Navy's Bureau of Medicine and Surgery. Weisberg sought Navy medical records tied to the Kennedy autopsy, and his request had to travel to the office that held them.

Referral memos are the plumbing of the Freedom of Information Act. A request arrives at the wrong desk; the agency routes it and notes the routing. This one preserves the path of a single request in February 1981, one step in a legal campaign Weisberg had already pursued for years. The memo shows an agency processing a critic's demand through channels, three decades of paperwork still to come.
nasa-tm-19660014325-go-no-go-for-apollo-:
F O Vonbun at Goddard derived a simple rule in November 1965 for a key Apollo question: should a mission go, or not go, based on how long its orbit will last? Orbital lifetime is set by air drag, which slowly pulls a low satellite down. A short predicted life could rule out a planned mission. Vonbun gives the go, no-go test in a clean analytic form.

He says a formula teaches more than a giant computer program does. A chart in the paper compares his quick slide-rule answers with computer results. Planners gained a check they could run by hand. In a program as complex as Apollo, simple cross-checks had real value against silent machine errors.
nasa-tm-19670013545-a-method-to-correct-:
Barbara Sparkman, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this method paper in February 1967. It fixes a calibration problem in a Nimbus medium resolution infrared radiometer flown on NASA's Convair 990 research aircraft. The instrument's three infrared channels read lower and lower as the aircraft climbed, so high-altitude measurements came out too low.

Sparkman's correction leans on the radiometer's built-in check-of-calibration cavity, whose temperature is tracked by an embedded thermistor. Assuming the whole calibration shifted by the amount that check indicates, degraded readings can be repaired. The paper derives the correction equations and describes a way to test them. Data checks gave good agreement with temperatures worked out from theory, once radiation passing through the atmosphere was accounted for. A closing section explains the physical cause of the shift.
nasa-tm-19700015446-cosmic-ray-diffusion:
Frank C. Jones of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint on how cosmic rays spread through space. Cosmic rays are fast particles that slowly diffuse, wandering as they cross a region of space. Jones checks a common shortcut in that work, the leakage lifetime approximation, and asks when it can be trusted.

His tool is an expansion of the solution in eigenfunctions, the natural patterns of the governing equation. Keeping only the lowest pattern gives the shortcut, and Jones shows where that move holds up. With energy losses such as synchrotron or inverse Compton losses, he finds, it cannot be justified. He also solves the general case where several energy effects act together.
the-healing-of-nations-and-the-hidden-so: Edward Carpenter wrote The Healing of Nations and the Hidden Sources of Their Strife. The book is dated 1915. A line from Revelation stands on the title page. It speaks of the tree of life and the healing of nations. The contents list seventeen chapters. Titles include War-Madness and The Roots of the Great War. Later titles include The Case Against Germany and The Case for Germany. An appendix is called A New and Better Peace. Nothing past the front matter is present here.
